lessons: Session 1: the reveal must be a punchline, not a page. Keep insight under 200 characters; the model line is the thing to remember.
Session 1: scenarios must fit anyone. Use school, friends, family, hobbies, phones and money before office situations. Avoid currency-specific amounts or use local-neutral ones.
Session 1: describe today's answers, never the person. 'You lean cautious today', not 'You are cautious'.
Session 1: give the player a win. Reveal games with a factual answer set `answer`; wrong picks get curious, kind feedback.
Session 1: a hook must add tension the game question doesn't repeat.
Session 1: order games feel like worksheets unless the order itself is surprising. Prefer choice/estimate for procedures.
Session 1: the research psychologist flagged overclaiming. Name effect sizes honestly and mark replication-hit findings 'contested'.
Session 1: deeper readers want a doorway to the primary text. Add from_source for classical ideas (public-domain translations).
Session 3: balance every scenario list across life stages: one school/young example, one work example, one home/family example. Too teen loses managers; too office loses teens.
Session 3: never claim 'most people' without a cited source. Estimate cards may set typical_miss: true only when explain cites how people usually guess.
Session 3: swipe prompts must not create double negatives: the left/right labels should answer the prompt directly.
Session 3: venn axis labels must be short (one or two words); put explanations in the question text.
Session 3: use currency-neutral amounts or none at all; avoid platform names that date a card (prefer 'your feed' over 'Facebook' unless it's the study).
Session 4: every game must end by showing what the player missed and why, not just a score.
Session 4: swipe labels should be self-explaining ('Thermostat (settles)' / 'Snowball (grows)'); keep jargon for the insight.
Session 4: order games only for genuinely surprising sequences of 3-4 short items; otherwise use choice.
Session 4: reveal games without a factual answer need a punchline in the reveal text itself (a real-life example), not 'no study exists'.
Session 5: never repeat a story (same study or anecdote) across two cards; each card owns its example.
Session 5: questionnaires (venn/radar) must earn their length: 3-4 questions and a personal frame (pick your goal first) beat 6 abstract items.
Session 5: put the verdict before the explanation on every game type.
Daily day 1 (Ollama): generated cards defaulted to office presentations; every new card needs a non-work scenario first.
Session 6: every step of a multi-step scenario must stay in the same life-world as step 1; don't jump from bedroom to boardroom mid-card.
Session 6: a swipe item's 'why' must agree with its side; never argue against your own answer.
Session 6: cautious choices are not character flaws; feedback on a 'safe' option explains the trade-off without judging the person.

Session 7: the audience pendulum swung too far to teen scenarios; a 44-year-old felt excluded. Each multi-step card: one school/young step, one work step, one home step. Single-step cards alternate across the domain.
Session 7: open with the surprise. Put the vivid relatable step first and history/philosophy references last ('Plot twist from real life').

Session 9: the teen-vs-manager tension is structural. Cards may live fully in one life-world now (school, work or everyday); the feed learns which one each player relates to. Don't mix worlds inside one card just to be fair.
Session 9: depth belongs before the Next button; reflective readers must not be pushed on before the reasoning.
Session 11: set "audience" explicitly on every card that is school-only or work-only; an "all" card must contain no office or school leftovers anywhere (try_today and try_team included).
Session 11: spread examples across hobbies (music, dance, gaming, cooking, languages), not mostly football.
Session 13: an "all" card must not contain a single line that assumes age or job (little brother, teacher, your teen, manager, savings). If it does, either neutralise it or set the card's audience.
Session 13: philosophy cards must reach the core teaching (Epictetus: judgments, not things, disturb us), not stop at the slogan.

Session 16: unreviewed local-model cards sank the panel (76 vs 84): reveal choices as objects ([object Object]), markdown asterisks, inflated 'strong' evidence on popular books, models that invert the concept (shifting the burden), and adult scenarios tagged 'all'. Every merged card must be rewritten to house standard and checked against the concept's real definition before it ships.
recent_problems: It leaves out Oettingen's key condition. Mental contrasting raises effort only when people already expect they can succeed. When expectations are low, it lowers commitment, which is by design: it helps people disengage. 'Modest but replicated' also overstates a mixed replication record. The Stockdale story comes second-hand through Collins and is not evidence, yet it shares the insight's first line with the research.

Survey-design error. The prompt asks a personal-preference question ('Who do you spend it with?') and then grades it with answer: 0. A player who honestly picks the book author is marked wrong for their own value. Fredrickson & Carstensen measured how often groups chose each option, not which choice was correct.

The reveal starts 'Many people can't' with no data behind it. It then cites affective forecasting, which concerns predicting future feelings (the impact or durability bias), not forgetting past worries, so the conclusion does not follow from the question. The impact bias is also partly a measurement artifact (Levine et al., 2012), so it needs a hedge. The three answer choices get no different feedback.

The 'Car crashes = more common than it feels' item conflicts with the classic data. In Lichtenstein et al. (1978), people overestimated accident deaths, motor vehicles included, relative to disease. The prompt 'Compared to how often it feels like it happens' is also ambiguous: feels to whom? Players are left guessing what the experimenter thinks. 'Strong' evidence for availability as the cause of risk misestimates also overstates it, because part of the pattern is regression toward the mean.

All six items are worded positively, so a tired or agreeable player who taps 'agree' everywhere lands in 'All Lights On' (acquiescence bias). The schema already supports invert:true but the card does not use it. 'I could do a rough version today' (Skill) also depends on time and access today, which is the Opportunity axis.

Bandura was clear that self-efficacy is task-specific, but the items refer to 'what I want to do' and 'this' without ever asking the player to pick a task, so the answers mix several domains. All 8 items are positively keyed. 'Evidence: strong' fits the four-source model, but the Body axis is really Jamieson's arousal reappraisal, which has more modest support.

Estimate cards start the slider at the midpoint of the range (20,300 weeks on four-thousand-weeks, 123 sec on attention-residue). If I just tap through without dragging, I still get a 'Plot twist: it's smaller.' reveal I didn't earn. The default position also leaks the direction: on both cards the answer sits far left. On the weeks card a linear 500 to 50,000 range means the real answer (4,174) sits in the first 7% of the track, so landing near it with a thumb is basically impossible, and step:2 is pointless at that scale.

After ordering, every placed chip turns the same teal whether it was right or wrong. The only feedback is a tiny orange monospace '→ step 4' that wraps onto its own line. Then the explain block repeats all five full item strings joined by arrows, which is a wall of text. The reward moment doesn't land and I can't see at a glance what I got wrong.

Every feedback line opens with 'Not the best move.' or 'Best move.' In the 3/3 screenshot that is already shown by the green and orange option borders, so it reads as a scolding stamp, 9 times in one card. The end banner 'Good instincts. One more trick below.' on 1/3 also doesn't match what happened.

The prompt asks a personal preference ('Who do you spend it with?') but then grades it with answer:0. Anyone who picks the author they loved gets marked wrong for an honest choice. The hook 'choose like their grandparents' is also hard to parse on first read.

The result shows 'Will 0/10 · Skill 0/10 · Opportunity 0/10' and a lone black dot floating outside all three circles at bottom left. It looks like a rendering bug, not a placement. Getting 0/0/0 on a goal I chose also feels deflating, even with the kind copy.

In all 4 questions the middle option is the reasonable one and the extremes are caricatures ('Go in trainers, no water'). It's a 'pick the middle' pattern that's solved after question 1, so there's no tension. circle-influence-spectrum has the same problem: the 'good' answer is obvious every time.
